Dermatology · published research

Laser skin resurfacing wounds and erythema

Small human studies report reduced redness or faster healing after some resurfacing procedures, while later controlled studies range from mixed to null. The evidence supports a possible short-term benefit for selected protocols but does not establish a consistently effective regimen.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small human studies report reduced redness or faster healing after some resurfacing procedures, while later controlled studies range from mixed to null. The evidence supports a possible short-term benefit for selected protocols but does not establish a consistently effective regimen.

Summary of the Evidence

Ten publications are grouped under laser-resurfacing wounds and erythema. Eight are human primary reports, one is a review, and one is a rat study. Seven human reports evaluate LED or laser PBM after resurfacing; one evaluates the fractional resurfacing laser itself and is not direct evidence for adjunctive PBM. Two favorable 2006 reports came from the same research group, and the available records do not establish whether their participants were independent.

Human and clinical evidence

Several early small split-face studies reported less redness or faster recovery on the light-treated side. In a 20-person study after fractional resurfacing, 590-nm amber-yellow LED treatment was followed by less erythema on the treated side at 24 hours (Alster and Wanitphakdeedecha 2009). A 10-person split-face study reported lower intensity and duration of redness after 635-nm red LED following fractional CO₂ resurfacing (Oh et al. 2013). Two small 2006 studies also reported faster healing with red, or combined red and near-infrared, LED after ablative resurfacing; cohort overlap between these reports is unclear (Trelles et al. 2006 Trelles et al. 2006).

Later findings are less uniform. In a 17-person split-face study, erythema duration was similar on treated and untreated sides, although some comparisons with a separate CO₂-only group favored LED (Wanitphakdeedecha et al. 2018). A small sham-controlled study found no significant difference in erythema or other skin measures (Duff et al., 2021). In 25 healthy volunteers, three wavelengths were tested after low-density fractional ablation on the inner arm. Reviewers more often selected treated images as faster healing, but the difference was not statistically significant, and pain, discomfort, and itch did not differ (Soliman et al. 2024). This model is not the same as facial cosmetic resurfacing.

Animal evidence

One rat experiment found faster recovery and better collagen remodeling when PBM followed fractional CO₂ laser treatment (Bueno et al., 2025). This supports a possible repair effect in that model, but it does not resolve the mixed human findings.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No indication-specific in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human studies used 590-nm amber-yellow, 633–635-nm red, 830-nm near-infrared, and, in a recent volunteer study, 465-nm blue, 640-nm red, and 880-nm near-infrared LEDs. Schedules ranged from a single post-procedure exposure to repeated sessions over several weeks. Doses, irradiance, resurfacing depth, treated body site, and postoperative care varied. No head-to-head dose-finding study identifies a preferred wavelength or schedule, and results from healthy arm skin cannot automatically be transferred to facial resurfacing.

Interpretation

Some small controlled studies found less short-term redness or faster healing, and one rat study found improved repair measures. Other human studies were mixed or showed no clear difference. A short-term erythema benefit is possible with selected protocols, but the literature does not yet establish how reliably it occurs or which parameters matter.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term reduction in post-resurfacing erythema Very low for faster wound healing and symptom relief
Publications and records10 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several small split-face studies found less redness or faster recovery, including randomized comparisons, so the favorable results should be stated directly. Later studies were mixed or found no clear difference, and one database record tested the resurfacing laser itself rather than adjunctive PBM. Larger trials with the same procedure, blinded assessments, and consistent redness and healing measures would clarify how often the benefit occurs.
